titleFa: کتاب Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
titleEn: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
author: Yuval Noah Harari
introFa: کتاب «Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind» نوشته Yuval Noah Harari یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: THE ORIGINAL BOOK “Sapiens” presents a pleasant and simple narrative about the extraordinary story of the evolution of mankind. In this work, it shows a detailed vision that everything we learn in school about history doesn’t teach us anything about how our species spread throughout the world. How big cities and empires occurred, what made us believe in Gods, why did money arise? From that curious and interesting past, we are also presented with a projection into the future, towards the millenniums to come. It is a well narrated chronical of life. From the first humans that inhabited the earth, all the way to the considerable progress like the great cognitive, agricultural and scientific revolutions. This work has drawn interest from universities and the public. Making the young writer an international celebrity.

CONTENT The Origin Humans And Their History A Singular Being The Expansion Inheritance From Gathering To Harvesting The Future Writing Culture Universal Order How Much Is It? The Imperial Vision The Scientific Revolution A Costly Union, Science And Technology Conquering Mentality A Bear Hug The Industrial Engine When Do I Fit In This History? Where Are We Heading? About The Author Of The Original Book About Sapiens Editorial

THE ORIGIN The Big Bang is one of the theories we have learned in school since we were kids, which is about the origin of matter and energy. It says that 13,500 million years ago, the universe was in a state of great intensity and then expanded. About 300,000 years later, matter and energy started combining complex structures, atoms, which at the same time united in molecules. 3,800 years ago, on planet Earth, some molecules combined shapes to form organisms, Homo Sapiens among them. 70,000 years prior, the species Homo Sapiens formed into more complex structures called cultures. The development of these cultures is called history. There are three important revolutions that marked history. Cognitive, which started around 70,000 years ago, the agricultural revolution, which became obvious about 12,000 years ago, and the scientific one, which only started 500 years ago. And just as expected, this history of revolutions and transformations affected humans and their way of organizing.

HUMANS AND THEIR HISTORY Eastern Africa is where the first humans appeared around two and a half million years ago. Descendants of Australopithecus (austral apes), left their native land and headed north of Africa to Europe and Asia. The geographical conditions of the places where they were established, required necessary adaptations for survival. Therefore, the populations evolved with unique features. As a result, a variety of species originated. Among them, Homo Neanderthalensis, commonly known as ‘Neanderthals’ were the humans in Europe and Western Asia. Homo Erectus, upright men, inhabited eastern Asia for two million years and it was the most enduring species known till now. Homo Sapiens, our species, arose 300,000 years ago and still dominates the planet in which all previous species have died out.

A SINGULAR BEING Aside from all the differences from comparing human species, there are also several common features. The most evident is the size of the brain. It is very large in comparison to other animals. It is two or three percent of our total body weight and it uses 25% of body energy. Another human feature is walking upright on two legs. It is a position that enables to look at far distances and it allows the hands to fall freely to be able to occupy them with something. The development of women in communities allowed for premature births. Although, due to the nature of dependency of offspring, the need for strong social bonds facilitated the development and education of humans born without any skills. A large brain, the use of utensils, superior learning capacities and complex social structures were the advantages that would turn mankind into the most powerful species on Earth. Many historic catastrophes were the consequence that humans were ambivalent of being superior but fearful inferiors. The fire was the first great discovery which opened an important gap between man and animals. It entitled man to really feel superior, for it gave the control of a potentially unlimited force.

THE EXPANSION Sapiens invaded Earth which lead to the dying out of other human species. The debate around the cause for this supremacy is open, and scientists have not come to an agreement yet. Some talk about a cross between species, others speak of extermination. Whatever the reason may be, the truth is that it is the species which boosted on the planet. Master of the world, Homo Sapiens began to produce culture, art, jewellery, religion, commerce and social strata; there are scientifically studied testimonies. These creations were the consequences of a revolution in Sapiens cognitive capabilities. A result, perhaps of genetic mutations which changed the internal wiring of the brain. This allowed them to think and communicate in a totally new way, giving way to the use of language. Two theories co-exist which try to explain the emergence of language in mankind. One of them considers that its upsurge was the natural evolutive path to benefit survival and reproduction, based on a tool of protection against predators and other dangers. The other one suggests that our language evolved as a means of sharing information about humans, according to which Homo sapiens are a social animal. Both theories are probably partially correct, but what makes our language unique is the ability to refer to things have never been seen or heard of before. With this cognitive revolution, legends, myths, Gods and religions came along. It forced Sapiens to live in a dual reality. In one hand, an objective and palpable reality, formed by trees, animals, lions, and on

the other hand, the reality imagined by the Gods, nations and associations. The latter one became stronger, up to the point of outweighing and controlling the first one. The world of representation was more determining than the world of tangible objects. As of that cognitive revolution, Sapiens started to rapidly change their behaviours and own their history. They passed their teachings onto newer generations, transforming social strata, the nature of its interpersonal relationships and their economic activities. They planned complex actions to avoid predators, gathering and stocking up on food, and created cooperative groups of mutual protection. They were no longer dependent on their environment. They ceased being controlled by it and they became the controllers.

INHERITANCE Evolutive psychology implies that most of our social and psychological characteristics were shaped and moulded during these times in the past, which hunting and gathering marked the minds of Sapiens. Our eating and sexual habits as well as our present conflicts, seem to be the product of a hunter-gatherer mind set, in a post-industrial environment of our times. The instinct of stuffing ourselves with food is deeply rooted in those genes. In sexual territory, the theory of ‘former commune’ attempts to explain how infidelities in modern marriage are traits we inherited from those social structures lacking private property, monogamous relationships and even paternity. In which a woman could have sexual relationships with several men and her children were offspring of the community; for no one knew exactly who the father was. This theory is rejected by scholars who insist that monogamy is a fundamentally historic human behaviour. The truth is that we have not found a unique way of life since the cognitive revolution for Sapiens, but cultural options before a palette of diverse opportunities and threats. Within this diversity, the norm consisted of a healthy diet proceeding from hunting and gathering, a short week of labour and very few infectious diseases. As a counterpart, mortality was high in infants, the unhealthy , people with different capacities or the elderly were sacrificed, as they were considered a burden to the tribe. Perhaps these were antecedents of abortion and euthanasia which generate great debate today.

What about spiritual life? Most scholars indicate that sapiens were animists. The belief in which almost all places, animals, plants and natural phenomenon’s have a consciousness and feelings and can communicate directly with humans. Animists believe there are no barriers between humans and other beings.

FROM GATHERING TO HARVESTING The hunting and gathering system changed about 10,000 years ago when Sapiens discovered they could manage plants and animals. They started sowing seeds and watering plants. They moved their animals towards grassland zones. It was a true revolution, the agricultural revolution. An original viewpoint considers that the agricultural revolution was a true disaster. It is true that the amount of food available throughout the year expanded, but it did not translate into a better way of feeding or more spare time; but in demographic explosions and spoiled elites. The average agriculturist worked harder than the average hunter- gatherer and in exchange they got a poorer diet. Many say that it was due to plants that adapted to Homo Sapiens and not the other way around. Plants among where wheat, rice and potatoes were found. The development of agriculture and domestication of animals was a gradual process which took centuries and millenniums. The shift happened in stages which changed costumes and life style little by little. Leaving the nomad life style behind allowed women to have one child per year, and the population started to grow in villages. Children started eating cereals and other solids at an early stage, ceasing breast-feeding which caused an outbreak of child mortality. One in every three children died before the age of twenty. However, the rise in births outnumbered deaths, therefore, the population grew. One law in history states that luxuries became necessities and this

generated new obligations. This law was applied to the economic system. More population required more food because the excess was not enough, therefore, they had to work more. The truth is, the agricultural revolution changed the intimate symbiosis that the Sapiens had with nature, and sowed the seed of greed.

THE FUTURE Hunters and gatherers didn’t take the time to think of the future. The agricultural revolution, in exchange, gave the future considerable space. The cycle and uncertainty of crops was the main motivator. Crops and plants were very limited and were at the mercy of storms, droughts, floods and pests; hence the human mind steered towards the future from which its livelihood depended on. Aside from worrying, the farmer started to think in terms of doing something about those issues. Working another field, digging another hole for irrigation and growing more plants. Their idea was to generate excessive production to have in case of adversities. Labour linked to agriculture had a transcendental aftermath. It was the foundation of political and social systems. Unfortunately, elites arose from it (governors, soldiers, priests and artists) who had power over peasants and only left them with the bare minimum to survive. With these appropriated riches, they built palaces, monuments and temples. Because of this, a social order arose.

WRITING New life styles started to generate enormous amounts of information linked to social order, commercial transactions and taxes; the brain was not large enough to store it all. With the emergence of complex societies, a new type of information was necessary, numbers. Mathematical information was vital to control income figures, possessions, payments, commercial exchanges, and a new system to record them was created, writing. This allowed to store data through symbols. The invention of scripture has been attributed to the Sumerians. Their system combined two types of symbols which were printed on clay tablets. One of those symbols was numbers and the others represented people, animals, goods, dates and geographical territories. By combining both types, facts and figures could be represented, only the indispensable, for writing required time and qualified readers were very few. Writing evolved with time and Sapiens wanted to write other things which didn’t only involve numeric facts. So, between 3000 and 2500 AD more symbols were added to the Sumerian system. This gave way to the cuneiform system. With it, acts were issued, oracles were registered and personal letters were written. Complex writing extended widely just like its usage.

CULTURE The complexity in human societies grew along with imaginary constructions, norms and laws which sustained social order. Myths and fictions became more familiar to people and these started behaving in a determined way, according to certain norms. This network of ‘artificial instincts’ is what we know as culture. Each human group had its own vision of the world and system of social, legal and political norms. These worked properly, but were in a flow of constant change. Where is the history of cultures heading? Adopting a new point of view of a cosmic satellite spy that observes millenniums, it is clear that history shifted towards unity. This fact can be appreciated when we count the number of separate ´human worlds´ that coexisted on planet Earth. Even if we think of our planet as a unity today, during a great part of history it was actually some kind of galaxy of many isolated human worlds which gradually merged throughout centuries. One global culture is not homogeneous, it contains many kinds of lifestyles and people. However, they´re all interconnected and mutually influence one another in multiple ways. They understand each other´s languages, they fight with the same weapons and move with the same interests.

UNIVERSAL ORDER The first millennium A.D witnessed the emergence of three universal orders which enabled the entire world and all of humanity to be considered as one single unit. First, there was the economic order, the monetary order. The second was political, the imperial order. The religious one was the third, the order of universal religions like Christianity, Buddhism and Islam. Not a single sector of Earth escaped its influence.

HOW MUCH IS IT? Life became more complex, and that complexity encompassed covering basic needs. Hunters-gatherers didn´t know what money was. Each tribe was self-sufficient. Their members shared goods and services in an economy of favours and obligations. If someone lacked meat, they´d ask their neighbours who would surely help them knowing a favour would be given back as payment. But with the development of agriculture, the system of favours became a barter system. Let’s see why. Due to its expansion and efficiency, agriculture facilitated coverage of the community’s food necessities. Free from the constant pressure of having to get food, just like in hunting and gathering, some people started developing new trades, like ironsmith and weaving. Each group specialized in something, with the improvement of transport, bartering spread and got different tribes involved and communities interconnected. As commercial activity continued to grow, bartering became more difficult since the supply of products turned out to be insufficient. For example, if a craftsman was trying to exchange a knife for a pig, what could he do if he didn’t have the knife to kill the pig and he didn’t have the pig? And what if he already had a lot of knives? He could commit to exchanging. But what if one of the parties didn’t stick to their side of the deal? Writing came to solve this problem by registering all transactions on tablets. To respond to the needs of economic activities which were becoming more intense, barley started to be used as a currency for payment, ‘money’. This currency for exchange was convertible into anything

which might be of necessity. Fixed amounts of barley were then established as a universal measure to exchange all other goods and services. But the greatest progress money made, was when people started to trust in it, even though it did not have any value. It was easier to carry and store. This new type of money appeared in ancient Mesopotamia in the third millennia A.D. It was shekels of silver, which wasn´t a coin but 8,33 grams of silver. In contrast to barley, which can be eaten, the shekel of silver was purely a cultural value. There was only one small step from them to coins.

THE IMPERIAL VISION The invention of scripture and the emergence of money facilitated life and transactions for a certain period of time. But simultaneously, societies and economies kept growing and therefore, becoming more and more complex. Regulating behaviour in people and creating systems of authority which attempted to ensure everyone kept in their place, became necessary. Hierarchy systems stemmed from empires, with a king or emperor, to whom everyone owed obedience. For example, the Hammurabi code, was created by the Babylonian king of the same name in 1776 BC. This code of laws established an order across the empire, registering what could and could not be done. The Hammurabi King legitimized his rule and his code, declaring himself designated by the Gods to rule Mesopotamia. If a superior entity, a God, endorsed power, then ruling was ensured. Empires multiplied and expanded like religions which increased power infinitely. Cultural diversity and territorial flexibility gave empires a fundamental role in history. The merged diverse ethnic groups under one political cloak, a union which caused reduction in human diversity, amalgamating many small cultures and merging them in a few big cultures. Since the year 200 AD, empires showed a global trend, and the imperial vision of ruling the entire world seems to be imminent. As the 21st century progressed, nationalism quickly lost ground. Increasingly, people think that protecting human rights and the interests of the whole human species must be the lighthouse that guides politics. The world is still politically divided, but states have

less interdependence with time. International and regional blocks, the signing of agreements involving all, are some of the characteristics shown that nations don´t have independent economic policies, opening global markets and respecting their standards. The global empire being forged is governed by a multiethnicity elite and its common interests keep them together. Worldwide, entrepreneurs, engineers, lawyers, experts and scholars are tempted to join the empire. They must evaluate if they respond to that call or stay loyal to their state. As time goes on, more are joining the empire.

THE SCIENTIFIC REVOLUTION Throughout the last 500 years, the history of mankind has witnessed a vertiginous growth in human power. In the year 1500 there were 500 million Homo Sapiens in the world. Today there is 7000 million. The flow of money, food and energy consumption increased exponentially. Humans began to think they could boost their abilities if they invested on scientific research. Thus, the submissive behaviour of humans who didn´t believe in the power of their own capacities but only in an almighty God began to change in the 16th and 17th centuries. A scientific revolution extended over Europe, and with it, people ceased hoping that everything would come from a God and dedicated to think and research with the objective of finding out how they could improve society through science. The scientific revolution has mostly been a revolution of ignorance. For the starting point was the discovery that humans don´t have an answer to the most important questions. This disposition to admitting ignorance has changed the ability to understand how the world works and to invent modern technologies. Through observation, exploration and experimentation, humanity fundamentally took epistemological leaps in fields like medicine, astronomy and physics with the goal that society would bring better living conditions. Throughout centuries, science has offered us many new tools. Some are mind related, like the ones used to foresee mortality and economic growth rates. Other tools are technological. In reality, the relationship between science and technology is quite

recent. Technological advances emerged by trial and error, not because of scientific studies. Science, industry and technology only intertwined with the arrival of the industrial revolution and the capitalist system. Without a doubt, once this relationship emerged, the world changed rapidly.

A COSTLY UNION, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY We live in the era of technology. Many are convinced that science and technology, united, can solve all our problems. We just need to encourage experts in both disciplines to carry on with their work. Let´s not be naive though. Science is a very expensive matter, and so is technology. Like every other field in culture, they´re shaped by economic, political and religious interests. Over the past 500 years, modern science has achieved wonders, thanks to the good disposition of governments, foundations and private donors who´ve donated millions of dollars to research. With this money, a lot has been done to explore the universe. Investments mostly, which behind the altruistic objectives, had one end goal of economic and political achievements , in summary, of power. The two forces which moved the world during the last 500 years are imperialism and capitalism. The everlasting link between science, the empire and capital was the motor.

CONQUERING MENTALITY Modern science flourished during the European empire. Although it adopted a few traditions from ancient Greece, China, India and Islam, it was only in a modern period of Spanish imperial expansion that it gained a unique and consolidated character. European imperialism was completely different to the rest in history. Europeans started to acknowledge that they didn´t know anything of what was out there beyond their borders, and therefore, set on expeditions to get answers. Conquered territory and knowledge intertwined stronger over time in such a way that expeditions brought scientists among their crew on voyages for scientific discoveries. The discovery of America was the highlight of the scientific revolution. The desire to conquer America pushed Europeans to find new beginnings. To control new territories they had to know a lot about history, geography, weather, flora, fauna, cultures and history of those new lands and their inhabitants. Europeans started to admit their ignorance. They drew maps with empty spaces which motivated new quests and conquests. The idea of progress, the development of research and science, enabled the establishment of new commercial routes. They prospered without interfering with the old ones, new goods were produced without making the existing ones obsolete. The economy shifted little by little due to the trust in the future. Credit emerged, which brought a large economic growth. This didn´t occur overnight but over an extended period, though it marked a solid direction.

A capitalist economy then unfolds, in which the concept of benefits having to be reinvested in production emerges. Adam Smith and his work ´The wealth of nations´ were revolutionaries in that sense. Smith ´s concepts were clear. New benefits were generated which were then reinvested in production, leading to more benefits infinitely. One new elite emerges and replaces nobility, stockbrokers and powerful businessmen move capital and invest to increase productivity. Smith says, greed is good and by becoming rich everyone benefits, not just oneself.

A BEAR HUG Very soon, capital and politics joined in one warm hug. They started to influence one another and generated debates on behalf of economists, politicians and public opinion. The notion of free market supported the concept that politics must reduce its participation in the economy to a minimum. In parallel, the inconveniences of capitalism of free market were noticed; it can´t be guaranteed that benefits are obtained fairly or equally distributed. The upsurge of communism and the fear of it settling, curbed ambitions and greed for profit a bit. This led the world toward more moderate postures and agreements which are beneficial for communities. Even though, occasionally we might doubt that they respond to everyone´s interests.

THE INDUSTRIAL ENGINE The truth is, global economy grows due to the trust in the future and reinvestment of profits of capital into production. But this is not sufficient. Energy and commodities are needed. If they run out, the entire system will collapse. Machines that allow you to convert one type of energy into another, the internal combustion engine, the electricity race are some of the milestones assigned to the industrial revolution. This was, in its core, a revolution in search for energy conversion which seems to have become unlimited. The availability of energy and abundant commodities led to a productive explosion. Peoples necessities and elegance, were creative inspirations, and products of all types and qualities stemmed from this. It was enough for people to want something and it would be available in the market. Consumerism followed. People were encouraged to treat themselves, and the urge of shopping settled in. Manufacturers design products of a short life span and invent newer models because we buy products with the means of being up to date with fashion. Shopping has become one of the most favourite pastimes of people.

WHEN DO I FIT IN THIS HISTORY? The history of mankind has been outlined in these pages. Incredible revolutions which shifted planet Earth, the economy and society. Science and the industrial revolution have been seen as the great and mighty in humanity. Consequently, social, political order and daily life have also been transformed. But the biggest question is, are we happier? Historians have avoided asking this question, and therefore, have not sought for the answer. They’ve researched the history of almost everything, but they haven’t stopped to ask in what manner have these issues influenced mankind’s happiness. Unfortunately, the answer is probably no. Why? Psychologists have played a key role in this study. Questionnaires of subjective wellbeing at the individual level have shown that levels of happiness go beyond the limits of general mundane things. It’s not the big events in history that have an impact on mankind’s happiness but the small things in our daily life. Homo Sapiens probably developed this balance between indulgence and unhappiness to ensure survival, to not fall into a traumatic event or cease looking for bigger and better opportunities. And it has been this way throughout time. Short periods of happiness altered by some depression is a constant in individuals. This has been the same during all periods of Sapiens, it does not depend on history. This depends and will depend on the ratios between objective conditions, outside the subjective conditions, between the expectations the and possibilities.

WHERE ARE WE HEADING? By the 21st century, Homo Sapiens have transcended the determining limits of biology and started to exploit the laws of nature and replace them with laws of intelligent design. Nowadays, there are three ways to do this substitution; biologic engineering, cyborgs engineering (beings which blend organic and non-organic parts) or through inorganic life engineering. Movies have taken charge in showing, as science fiction, which isn’t so much fiction, that they already exist in real laboratories. The real potential of science and technology will be able to change Homo Sapiens. New medical, ethical and social dilemmas are on their way. Is there a new human kind, maybe even better to the one we know, being generated? Let’s imagine an eternally young cyborg that doesn’t reproduce, has no sexuality, can exchange thoughts directly with other beings, has infinitely superior capacities to ours and its emotions differ from ours. Could we, Sapiens, live amongst them? Dating back to 70,000 years ago, Homo Sapiens were an insignificant animal taking care of his own life. Nowadays, it’s on the verge of becoming a God, a pivot between gaining eternal youth and immortality, the celestial capabilities of creation and destruction Are Sapiens responsible enough to take on this role? Time will tell.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR OF THE ORIGINAL BOOK Yuval Noah Harari is an Israeli writer, of Lebanese descendance, born in 1976. Specialized in medieval and military history, he received his doctorate at the University of Oxford, in England. Since then, he’s been focused on writing and has published numerous books and articles regarding military affairs of the Middle Ages. His work ‘Sapiens’ was the one that led him to fame. In 2015, Mark Zuckerberg, founder of Facebook, suggested his thirty-eight thousand contacts to read this book, presenting it as the great wonder of the history of humanity. Ever since, it has become a best seller worldwide.

ABOUT SAPIENS EDITORIAL Books are mentors. Books can guide what we do and our lives. Many of us love books while reading them and maybe they will echo with us a few weeks after but 2 years later we can’t remember if we have read it or not. And that’s a shame. We remember that at that time, the book meant a lot to us. Why is it that 2 years later we have forgotten everything? That’s not good. This summary is taken from the most important themes of the original book. Most people don’t like books. People just want to know what the book says they have to do. If you trust the source you don’t need the arguments. So much of a book is arguing its points, but often you don’t need the argument if you trust the source you can just get the point. This summary takes the effort to distill the blahs into themes for the people who are just not going to read the whole book. All this information is in the original book.
